summary:
Hello from Out There! is an interactive children’s storybook that tells the story of NASA’s exploration through the robots left behind on the Moon, Mars and in deep space. Aimed at ages 8 to 11, it is built as 13 letters, each written in the voice of a real mission (Surveyor 3, Apollo 11, 12 and 15, Viking 1, Pathfinder, Spirit and Opportunity, InSight, Ingenuity, NEAR Shoemaker, Dawn, Pioneer 10 and Kepler). Every letter pairs NASA-sourced science with a hands-on activity that earns a stamp in an "Explorer Passport". Our site also has a “Where Are They Now?” map and a Robot Family Tree.

It answers the challenge by giving each piece of abandoned hardware a voice, showing how each mission passed knowledge to the next. Last but not least, our main goal is for children to become more interested in STEM, as well as showing our readers that people are as capable as their goals and that the robots they meet were built by people who were once curious kids.
details:
Hello from Out There! is an interactive children’s storybook for ages 8 to 11, where real NASA robots left on the Moon, Mars and deep space write letters to the reader, in their own voice. The book has 13 letters in 4 chapters (the Moon, Mars, deep space and "your mission"). They cover Surveyor 3, Apollo 11, 12 and 15, Viking 1, Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, InSight, Ingenuity, NEAR Shoemaker, Dawn, Pioneer 10 and Kepler.

Each letter has a “Real Science” box with facts from NASA mission records. Each also has a hands-on “Try It” activity and a “You Can Too” line that connects the robot’s story to the child’s own potential. Finishing one of our interactive activities earns a stamp in our readers "Explorer Passport" and collecting all 13 unlocks a personalized Explorer Certificate they can download.

Other features:

Mission Postmaster (who is an owl guide who introduces the book and encourages kids to ask “What if?”)

Where Are They Now? (which is a map of 14 pins showing whether each robot is asleep, retired or still traveling.)

Robot Family Tree (shows how each mission passed knowledge to the next, like a relay race.)

Your Mission (our closing activity where the child designs their own explorer robot, name it and can also download it.)

Our aim is for kids to learn real mission history and science through story and play instead of a textbook.

Every fact is traceable to NASA mission records, including the NSSDCA catalog and NASA Science pages.

It builds early STEM habits, such as asking questions and testing ideas.

Accessibility is built in with a skip-to-content link, image alt text, a text-size control, and a layout that works on phones and tablets. It is also written at a reading level for 10-year-olds.

It is free and needs no login, so teachers and families can use it right away!!!

We want every child to finish the book believing that people are as capable as their goals and the robots are the proof of this! Each mission built on the one before it (Surveyor 3 helped prepare the Apollo landings, and Viking was a step toward the Mars missions that followed). These machines were built by people who started as curious kids and with our book, we want to invite the reader to become one of them. The aim is to spark early interest in STEM careers and show that space exploration is a story anyone can join.

We used; Base44 (AI app builder) to build the website (Base44 generates React and JavaScript, and the content is stored in one data file), Claude (Anthropic) helped draft the story text and the prompts used to build the site, as well as helped organize the research, AI image tools generated the illustrations (and each carries a visible “AI-generated” watermark.) This is stated on the About page, in the site metadata and in a code comment. The site uses no NASA logos, flags or mission patches and it states that it is not an official NASA product. We did not use any special hardware, it runs in any modern browser.

Instead of reciting facts about hardware, the machines speak as characters. This ties into the challenge’s idea of hardware that is “left behind but not forgotten.”

The robots are also connected as a chain of mission pioneers passing the torch, which gives a broad story of NASA exploration. Our book looks like a picture book but plays like an adventure, with stamps, a passport, a map and a certificate, where kids become the next chapter (as the last activity has the child design their own robot and see themselves as part of the story.)

The following factors should also be noted;

Our audience are kids ages 8 to 11.

All claims were limited to what NASA’s own pages support.

Responsible AI use, where we made all visible watermarks on all AI images, clear disclosure of where AI was used and no NASA branding, as the challenge rules required.

For child safety, no sign-ins or personal data collection from kids is needed. Passport stamps are only saved on the child’s own device.
